beats.narration_says: Three brothers shook three lots in a helmet. Whatever each of them drew, he would rule it forever.

To understand how the universe came to be divided that way, start with their father. Cronus ruled everything, and Cronus was afraid. He had been told that one of his children would overthrow him, exactly as he had overthrown his own father.
So he found a solution. Every time his wife Rhea gave birth, he took the child and swallowed it.
Hestia. Demeter. Hera. Hades. Poseidon. Five children, alive, inside him.
When the sixth was coming, Rhea hid. She gave birth in a cave on Crete, and handed her husband a stone wrapped in a baby's blanket. He swallowed it without looking. The child was Zeus.
Grown, he came back and forced his father to bring up everything he had eaten.
The stone came first. Then his brothers and sisters, one at a time, undamaged.
What followed was a war that lasted ten years, and neither side could finish it.
So Zeus went down into the pit beneath the world and let out the prisoners kept there.
Three one-eyed smiths made the weapons: a thunderbolt for Zeus, a trident for Poseidon, and for Hades a cap that made its wearer invisible.
Three giants with a hundred arms each ended the fighting, and the Titans took their place in the pit.
And then the winners had a problem. They had won a universe, and no agreement about who owned it.
They did not fight over it. According to Homer, they drew lots.
Poseidon drew the sea. Hades drew the mist and the dark. Zeus drew the wide sky.
One part was left out of the draw on purpose. The earth, and Olympus itself, stayed common to all three.
The place they all cared about most was the one place nobody won.
Zeus took the sky, and with it something more useful than weather.
He became the god of the oath and of the stranger at the door — the rules that let strangers deal with each other at all.
His weapon had been a gift from prisoners. His real power was the arrangement itself.
Poseidon drew more of the world's surface than either brother, and never accepted the result.
In the Iliad he tells a messenger that they drew equally, that they are equals, and that Zeus has no right to give him orders. Then he backs down, because Zeus is the elder.
Which is strange. Hesiod has Zeus born last of the six. Neither poem explains the difference.
Hades drew worst. He got the dead, and a kingdom with no sky in it.
He does not live on Olympus, and he is not one of the twelve who sit there.

The Greeks were uneasy enough about him that they mostly avoided saying his name, and built him almost nothing under that name — one sanctuary, opened one day a year, with only the priest allowed inside.
What they called him instead was Plouton. The rich one.

Because the dead were not all he had drawn. Everything that comes out of the ground comes out of his kingdom — the silver in the mines, the gold, and the seed that goes under the soil in autumn and comes back up in spring.
The brother who drew the darkness ended up holding the wealth of the world.
And every person who has ever lived arrives, eventually, in his share of it.
The full story of that draw is in the previous part. The sisters got no kingdom.
They got something smaller, and closer to home: a marriage, a harvest, and a fire in the middle of the house.
Hera married the winner. She became queen of the gods and goddess of marriage — married to the least faithful husband in Greek myth.
She could not punish Zeus, so she went after the women he loved, and their children.
Once she had Zeus put to sleep and sent a storm after his son Heracles. Zeus woke in a rage.
He hung her from the sky, a golden chain on her wrists and two anvils tied to her feet.
And yet the Greeks never treated her as the loser. At Olympia, Zeus's own sanctuary, her temple stood for more than a century before his.
And in one town in Arcadia she had three shrines: to Hera the Girl, Hera the Wife, and Hera the Widow — from the time she quarrelled with Zeus and went home.
A widow, with a husband who could never die.
Demeter got the grain. With Zeus she had a daughter, Persephone.
One day the girl was picking flowers when the ground split open, and Hades drove up in a golden chariot and carried her down to the dead.
Zeus, her own father, had promised her to him — without a word to her mother.
For nine days Demeter searched the earth with a torch in each hand, without eating or washing.
Then the Sun, who sees everything, told her the truth. Hades was her own brother, he said, a fitting husband — lord of the third share he drew when the world was divided.
She did not accept it. She left Olympus, sat down in her temple at Eleusis, and stopped the grain.
For a whole year nothing grew; oxen dragged ploughs through the fields for nothing.
Mankind was starving, and the gods were about to lose their sacrifices.
Zeus sent a messenger, then every god on Olympus, one after another, bearing gifts.
She refused them all. Nothing would grow until she saw her daughter.
And the king of the sky gave in.
He sent Hermes to bring Persephone back, and Hades let her go — but first he slipped her a single pomegranate seed.
She had eaten in the land of the dead, so for a third of every year she would return below.
Only then did Demeter let the fields grow again.
The sister with no kingdom had made the king of the sky back down, and the king of the dead give back what he had taken.
Hestia got the fire. She was the first child Cronus swallowed, and the last to come back up.
Poseidon and Apollo both asked to marry her.
She laid her hand on Zeus's head and swore never to marry at all.
So instead of a husband, Zeus gave her a place: the middle of every house.
The first offering at every feast went to her, and the last.
Greek cities kept a public hearth, and when colonists sailed off to found a new city, they carried its fire with them.
She has almost no myths of her own. In Plato, when the gods ride out across heaven, Hestia alone stays home.
The brothers drew three places where no living person can stay.
The sisters got the places where people live.
Every human life ends in Hades' kingdom. It is lived in theirs.
Zeus had overthrown a father who swallowed his own children.
Then he took a wife — and heard the same prophecy his father had heard.
Her name was Metis, and she was wiser than any god or mortal.
Earth and Sky, the same two who had warned Cronus, told Zeus what she would bear.
First a daughter, his equal in strength and judgment.
Then a son, who would be king of gods and men.
Zeus did not wait for the son. He tricked Metis with soft words, and swallowed her whole.
His father had swallowed the children, and one got away.
Zeus swallowed the mother. But the daughter was already inside her.
In time, Zeus gave birth to her himself — out of his own head.
Later poets say it took an axe to split it open.
Out leapt a grown woman in golden armour, shaking a spear.
Olympus shook, the sea heaved, and the Sun stopped his horses in the sky until she took the armour off.
This was Athena. Her mother's name meant cunning wisdom, and Athena became its goddess, in craft and in war.
And Metis never left. Hesiod says Zeus kept her inside him, to counsel him on good and evil.
When the gods chose their cities, Athena and her uncle Poseidon both wanted Athens.
He struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident, and salt water welled up. She planted an olive tree.
The gods gave her the city, and Poseidon, the brother who never accepted his share, flooded the plain in anger.
The daughter of the swallowed wife became her father's favourite — in one Athenian tragedy, the only god trusted with the keys to his thunderbolt.
Hera could not stop a child born from her husband's head. A child carried by another woman was different.
Leto was pregnant with Zeus's twins, and Hera hunted her across the earth.
Land after land turned her away; none dared let her give birth.
At last she reached Delos — a bare rock that, in some tellings, floated loose on the sea.
Even Delos was afraid the god would despise it and kick it into the waves.
So Leto swore an oath: his temple would make Delos rich forever.
Her labour lasted nine days and nine nights.
Every great goddess came — except Hera, who kept the goddess of childbirth beside her on Olympus.
The others sent a messenger to fetch her in secret, with a bribe: a golden necklace, nine cubits long.
The moment she set foot on Delos, Leto threw her arms around a palm tree, the earth laughed beneath her, and the child sprang out into the light.
It was Apollo. The whole island blossomed with gold, and the newborn god spoke at once.
The lyre and the bow would be his, he said, and he would tell mankind the will of Zeus.
In a later telling, his twin sister Artemis was born first — and helped her mother deliver him.
She grew up a hunter, unmarried, at home in the wild.
Her mother had been turned away by every land on earth.
Now every woman in labour called on her.
Apollo founded his oracle at Delphi, where he killed the serpent that lived there.
For a thousand years, cities asked him what was coming before they went to war or founded colonies.
And at Delphi, Hesiod says, Zeus had set up the stone his father swallowed in his place.
The god of prophecy kept the stone where this whole story began.
Centuries later, Athens ruled that no one could be born on Delos, or die there.
The one land that let Leto give birth became the one place in Greece where nobody could.
None of the three was supposed to be born.
One came out of her father's head and ended up holding the keys to his thunderbolt.
Two came off a drifting rock and became the goddess of birth and the voice of prophecy.
The only child who never came was the son who would have been king.
His mother is still inside Zeus.
So, Hesiod says, she answered in anger.
She bore a son of her own, without Zeus — Hephaestus, who would become the greatest craftsman among the gods.
But he was born lame, and Hera was ashamed of him. She threw him off Olympus.
Two sea goddesses caught him as he fell.
For nine years he lived in a cave beneath the waves, making jewellery for them, and no other god knew he was alive.
A later tradition says he took his revenge.
When he was grown, he sent his mother a gift: a golden throne.
Hera sat down, and invisible chains closed around her. She could not stand.
Hephaestus refused to come to Olympus and free her.
He would listen to no god except one — the god of wine, who made him drunk and led him up the mountain. Hera went free.
In time, Olympus needed him. He built the houses the gods lived in, and servants of gold that could think, and speak.
He married Aphrodite, the most beautiful of the goddesses.
Homer's Odyssey tells what came next, in a song a blind poet sings at a king's feast.
Aphrodite loved another: Ares, the god of war.
He was Hera's other son — Hephaestus's own brother — the swiftest god on Olympus, and the one Zeus said he hated most.
Once, two giants had chained him in a bronze jar for thirteen months, until Hermes stole him out.
But the Sun sees everything. Helios saw the two of them together, and went straight to Hephaestus. Hephaestus went to his forge.
He hammered out chains as fine as spider webs — too fine for any god to see, too strong for any god to break.
He fixed them around his bed, and hung them from the roof beams.
Then he announced that he was leaving for Lemnos.
Ares had been watching the house. He came at once.
The two lay down together — and the chains closed around them, and neither could lift a limb.
Hephaestus turned back before Lemnos. He stood in his doorway and called for Zeus and every god to come and see something laughable and unbearable.
Aphrodite, he said, had always scorned him for his lame leg, and loved Ares because Ares was handsome and sound of foot.
He demanded that Zeus give back every gift he had paid for her.
The goddesses stayed at home, out of shame.
The gods came — Poseidon, Apollo and Hermes.
Apollo asked Hermes whether he would take such chains for a night with golden Aphrodite.
Hermes said he would take three times as many, with every god looking on.
The gods roared with laughter. "Bad deeds do not prosper," one said.
"The slow one has caught the swift. Lame as he is, Hephaestus has caught the swiftest god on Olympus — by craft."
Only Poseidon did not laugh.
He begged Hephaestus to let Ares go, and promised that if Ares ran without paying, Poseidon himself would pay.
Hephaestus could not refuse him, and undid the chains.
Ares fled to Thrace. Aphrodite went to Cyprus.
Hesiod gives the two of them three children: Fear, Panic and Harmony.
Hephaestus could never outrun anyone, so twice he built a trap instead: a throne for his mother, and a net for his wife.
Both times he caught them. And both times, in the end, he let them go.
